summary.text: The Local Group is the galaxy group that includes the Milky Way, shaped like a dumbbell with the Milky Way and its satellites at one end and the Andromeda Galaxy and its satellites at the other.
The two halves are about 800 kiloparsecs apart and are moving toward one another at 123 km/s.
It has 134 known members, most of them dwarf galaxies, and it belongs to the Virgo Supercluster, which is part of the Laniakea Supercluster.

paragraphs.heading: Our galaxy's group
paragraphs.text: The Local Group is the group of galaxies that contains the Milky Way, and so contains Earth. It is shaped like a dumbbell with two lobes: one is the Milky Way with its satellite galaxies, and the other is the Andromeda Galaxy with its own satellites. The two lobes are about 800 kiloparsecs apart, and they are closing in on each other at 123 km/s.

paragraphs.heading: Size and setting
paragraphs.text: The center of the group lies about 1.5 million light-years from the Milky Way, a little nearer to Andromeda, which may be the more massive of the two. In total the group holds on the order of 2×10¹² solar masses and spans about 17 million light-years. It sits inside ever larger structures: the Local Volume, the Virgo Supercluster, and the still bigger Laniakea Supercluster.

paragraphs.heading: Who belongs
paragraphs.text: Nobody knows exactly how many galaxies are members, because the Milky Way hides some of them from view. So far 134 members are known within 1 megaparsec of the center, and most are dwarf galaxies. The Triangulum Galaxy, M33, is the third-largest member and the third spiral, at about 5×10¹⁰ solar masses. It is unclear whether it is a companion of Andromeda; the two are 750,000 light-years apart, and a close pass 2 to 4 billion years ago set off star formation across Andromeda's disk.

paragraphs.heading: Fuzzy edges
paragraphs.text: Some members, such as IC 10, IC 1613 and the Phoenix and Tucana dwarf galaxies, are probably not tied to either big subgroup. Farther out, membership gets uncertain: NGC 3109 and its companions are so far from the center that they may not count. The Antlia-Sextans Group is probably not bound to the Local Group by gravity, since it likely lies outside the group's zero-velocity surface. If so, it is a separate galaxy group of its own.

paragraphs.heading: Hubble's name
paragraphs.text: Edwin Hubble coined the name the Local Group in his 1936 book The Realm of the Nebulae. He described it as a typical small group, isolated from its surroundings. He listed its members in order of falling brightness, starting with M31, the Milky Way and M33, then the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, M32, NGC 205 and four others. He also marked IC 10 as a possible member.

paragraphs.heading: A merger ahead
paragraphs.text: Over tens of billions of years, the group's galaxies are likely to pull together under their shared gravity into one elliptical galaxy. The main event in that process will be Andromeda and the Milky Way joining. Astronomers still argue about the details. The merged galaxy might be elliptical right after the collision, or it might keep a spiral form for a while first, and some even suggest a lasting superspiral or a lenticular galaxy instead.
